CIVIL APPELLATE, JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 73 of 1950 [COURT_RECORDED]: Civil Appeal No. 73 of 1950 arises from a judgment of the High Court of Judicature at Patna dated 26th January, 1944, which itself stemmed from a decree of the Additional Subordinate Judge of Hazaribagh in Title Suit No. 45 of 1939.
Recorded scope: Case jurisdiction and procedural history defined; 1952 [CASE_IDENTIFIER]; Civil Appeal No. 73 of 1950. Court: Court of the Additional Subordinate Judge of Hazaribagh. Participants: not specified in this record. Property: not specified in this record.

BHAGWATI J [COURT_RECORDED]: The central legal question is whether, prior to the 1929 enactment of Section 65-A of the Transfer of Property Act, a mortgagor in possession had the power to grant a permanent lease of the mortgaged property so as to bind the mortgagee.
Recorded scope: Legal question for consideration identified; October 23, 1952 [EVENT_DATE]; Civil Appeal No. 73 of 1950. Court: High Court of Judicature at Patna. Participants: not specified in this record. Property: not specified in this record.

Narrative of Facts [COURT_RECORDED]: Raja Nilkanth Narain Singh mortgaged Gadi Sirampur to the Chota Nagpur Banking Association Limited on 1st August, 1914. The Bank obtained a mortgage decree on 29th November, 1921, and purchased a third share on 28th October, 1922.
Recorded scope: Mortgage and subsequent decree details; 1914 to 1922 [EVENT_DATE]; Original Mortgage Suit. Court: Court of the Additional Subordinate Judge of Hazaribagh. Participants: not specified in this record. Property: not specified in this record.

Narrative of Facts [COURT_RECORDED]: During the pendency of mortgage proceedings, on 5th November, 1925, Wazir Narain Singh granted a permanent lease of four villages to Hiraman Ram, Manager and Karta of his joint Hindu family, and his son Chohan Ram.
Recorded scope: Permanent lease granted during mortgage suit pendency; 5th November, 1925 [EVENT_DATE]; Court of Additional Subordinate Judge of Hazaribagh. Court: Court of the Additional Subordinate Judge of Hazaribagh. Participants: not specified in this record. Property: not specified in this record.

Narrative of Facts [COURT_RECORDED]: An agreement was made that if Wazir Narain Singh paid Rs. 1,10,631-4-0 by 16th August, 1926, the sale would be set aside. He executed a mortgage on 14th August, 1926, to the Court of Wards to satisfy dues and set aside the sale.
Recorded scope: Sale set aside and new mortgage executed; 1926 [EVENT_DATE]; Execution proceedings. Court: Court of the Additional Subordinate Judge of Hazaribagh. Participants: not specified in this record. Property: not specified in this record.

Narrative of Facts [COURT_RECORDED]: The Plaintiff (through the Manager of the Court of Wards) filed a suit on 4th February, 1929, to enforce the mortgage, impleading Hiraman Ram and Dilo Ram as co-defendants. A final decree for sale was passed on 18th September, 1931.
Recorded scope: Enforcement suit and auction sale; 1929 to 1935 [EVENT_DATE]; Suit for enforcement of mortgage. Court: Court of the Additional Subordinate Judge of Hazaribagh. Participants: not specified in this record. Property: not specified in this record.

Narrative of Facts [COURT_RECORDED]: Dilo Ram died after the mortgage decree. Hiraman Ram and his son Chohan Ram continued in actual possession. The Plaintiff filed the suit on 16th November, 1939, against them for khas possession of the villages.
Recorded scope: Suit for khas possession filed; 16th November, 1939 [EVENT_DATE]; Court of Additional Subordinate Judge of Hazaribagh. Court: Court of the Additional Subordinate Judge of Hazaribagh. Participants: not specified in this record. Property: not specified in this record.

Defendant 2 [PARTY_CLAIM]: Defendant 2 contended that the Plaintiff was not subrogated to the Bank's position, the decree was not binding as he was not a party, the Patta was not ended by the auction sale, and a partition occurred within a year allotting properties to him.
Recorded scope: Defendants contesting plaintiff's claim; During trial [EVENT_DATE]; Trial Court. Court: Court of the Additional Subordinate Judge of Hazaribagh. Participants: not specified in this record. Property: not specified in this record.

Trial Court [COURT_RECORDED]: The Trial Court held the Plaintiff was subrogated to the Bank's position, Defendant 1 was the Manager/Karta, Defendant 2 was fully represented, the decree was binding, and the Plaintiff was entitled to recover possession and mesne profits.
Recorded scope: Trial Court judgment delivered; Prior to 1944 [JUDGMENT_DATE]; Court of Additional Subordinate Judge of Hazaribagh. Court: Court of the Additional Subordinate Judge of Hazaribagh. Participants: not specified in this record. Property: not specified in this record.

High Court of Judicature at Patna [COURT_RECORDED]: The High Court negatived the contention regarding constructive res judicata. It considered whether Wazir Narayan Singh had power to grant the permanent lease, concluding the lease did not render the Bank's security insufficient under Section 66.
Recorded scope: High Court judgment dismissing plaintiff's suit; 26th January, 1944 [JUDGMENT_DATE]; High Court of Judicature at Patna. Court: High Court of Judicature at Patna. Participants: not specified in this record. Property: not specified in this record.

High Court of Judicature at Patna [COURT_RECORDED]: The High Court held the lease was valid and not affected by the Plaintiff's mortgage, decree, or execution sale, and accordingly dismissed the Plaintiff's suit. The Plaintiff obtained leave to appeal to the Privy Council.
Recorded scope: Final High Court decision and Privy Council admission; Prior to 1946 [JUDGMENT_DATE]; High Court of Judicature at Patna. Court: High Court of Judicature at Patna. Participants: not specified in this record. Property: not specified in this record.

Privy Council [COURT_RECORDED]: The Privy Council found the Plaintiff was subrogated to the Bank's position and Defendant 2 was sufficiently represented. The only surviving question was whether Wazir Narayan Singh had the power to grant a permanent lease to bind the Plaintiff.
Recorded scope: Privy Council identifies sole legal question; 1952 [EVENT_DATE]; Privy Council. Court: High Court of Judicature at Patna. Participants: not specified in this record. Property: not specified in this record.

H5b5bde33ed980a76.reason: Historical case involves mortgagee settlements creating occupancy rights, distinct from the current mortgagor lease validity test under pre-1929 law.
H5b5bde33ed980a76.assessed_historical_position: The mortgage was redeemed in June 1942 by payment in proceedings under section 83 of the Transfer of Property Act, When the plaintiffs went to take possession, they were resisted by the Gopes (defendant first party), and after unsuccessful criminal proceedings, the plaintiffs filed the present suit.: Plaintiffs redeemed mortgage in June 1942 but were resisted by Gopes (Defendant 1) upon taking possession, leading to this suit after failed criminal proceedings. The Subordinate Judge dismissed it, holding that the Gopes were raiyats having acquired permanent occupancy rights in the lands as the result of the settlement by the mortgagee, Lakhandeo Singh.: Subordinate Judge dismissed suit holding Gopes were raiyats with permanent occupancy rights from settlement by mortgagee Lakhandeo Singh. On appeal the High Court set aside this decision and gave the plaintiffs a decree for possession on the finding that the defendants were not raiyats and had no permanent rights of occupancy.: High Court set aside Subordinate Judge's decision, granting plaintiffs possession decree finding defendants were not raiyats with no permanent occupancy rights. At the trial, the plaintiffs alleged and maintained that the lands were their zirat lands within the meaning of section 116 of the Bihar Tenancy Act and that the defendant first party could acquire no rights of occupancy in the same.: Plaintiffs alleged lands were their zirat lands under Bihar Tenancy Act section 116, preventing defendants from acquiring occupancy rights. The Subordinate Judge found against this contention and held that they were khud kasht or bakasht lands of the proprietor, in which rights of occupancy can be acquired.: Subordinate Judge found against plaintiffs, holding lands were khud kasht or bakasht proprietor lands where occupancy rights can be acquired. It was held by the Privy Council in Bengal Indigo Company v. Roghobur Das that a zuripeshgi lease is not a mere contract for the cultivation of the land at a rent, but is a security to the tenant for the money advanced.: Privy Council in Bengal Indigo Company v. Roghobur Das held zuripeshgi lease is security for money advanced, not mere cultivation contract.

H705caa40b1cc6090.reason: Historical case addresses factual joint family status under Hindu law, whereas the current case requires application of the Transfer of Property Act regarding lease validity.
H705caa40b1cc6090.assessed_historical_position: Reporting Court: The court rejects the appellants' claim that a 1898 document proves Ram Narain and Ram Saran were joint owners, noting the property locations and areas differ from earlier joint records. Reporting Court: Documents from 1905 show Ram Narain and Ram Saran conducting joint business for 20 years, leading the High Court to infer they likely became a flourishing joint concern. Reporting Court: The court questions whether later documents showing joint conduct can destroy the inference of separation drawn from earlier documents, noting they lived like a joint family due to kinship. Reporting Court: The court holds that a statement in a lease deed describing Ram Narain and Ram Saran as joint does not contradict an earlier mortgage stating all three brothers were separated. Reporting Court: The court notes a sale deed by a stranger vendor recited the purchasers were uncle and nephew forming a joint family, which is described as somewhat surprising. Reporting Court: The court concludes that a proper consideration of all sale deeds does not necessarily lead to the conclusion that there was no original separation between the parties.

Hbfeed5caa95a711f.reason: Historical case relies on Section 53-A which did not exist in 1925, so its legal reasoning regarding written contracts cannot directly apply to the current statutory framework.
Hbfeed5caa95a711f.assessed_historical_position: The High Court of Bombay: The High Court of Bombay allowed the plaintiffs' appeal, decreeing the suit for survey Nos. 223 and 225 but dismissing it for Nos. 222 and 226, holding the plaintiffs entitled to sue as ijaradar or assignees. The Supreme Court of India: The Supreme Court held that the defendant's admission of paying rent for all 100 Dakdas to the plaintiff for three fields establishes the plaintiff's right to sue, regardless of title proof. The Supreme Court of India: The Supreme Court declined to decide if a signed contract existed under Section 53-A, ruling the Government Resolution was not evidence of such a contract due to lack of reasonable certainty. The Supreme Court of India: The Supreme Court affirmed the Assistant Judge's decision under Section 53-A, finding no substantial grounds to reverse it, though it deemed a full argument on the notice issue unnecessary. The Supreme Court of India: Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act (1929) provides a statutory defense allowing a transferee in possession to resist eviction by the transferor if a written contract exists and part-performance is shown. The Supreme Court of India: The Supreme Court noted that to satisfy Section 53-A, it must be proved that the Talukdari Settlement Officer contracted to lease the land via a writing signed by him with ascertainable terms.
